The \LFE, illustrated in @fig-illustration(a), and \NFZ, illustrated in @fig-illustration(b), 
are constructed using the proposals of (respectively)
new \removals and new \infections. These are obtained from the \history of the previous epidemic; the constructions also use

(i) (for the \NFZ) the set of new in\activated \removals,
(ii) and (for the \LFE) the set of new in\activated \infections.


::: {#fig-illustration layout="[[1,1]]"}

![Updating to new \removals and new \NFZ.](fig-update-removals){#fig-update-removals}

![Updating to new \infections and new \LFE.](fig-update-infections){#fig-update-infections}

Illustration of interaction of \NFZ and new \removals, 
and \LFE and new \infections.
:::


For simplicity we assume no conditioned removal at process-time \(0\).

:::{.callout-warning #wrn-no-conditioned-removal}
### Assumption of "no conditioned removal"
**\textcolor{red}{Can this assumption be lifted without pain?}**

(See also @cau-first-removal!)
:::

### Choice of initial number of \infectives

The first step is to show that the requirement for an initial number of infectives to generate an
epidemic activating precisely the conditioned \removals is that:

(a) the initial number is not less than the initial number of \LFE infectives  
\({}^\text{slow \LFE}I_{0-}{=}{}^\text{slow}\LFEInit\);
(b) the initial number is strictly less than the intersection of \NFZ with the \(t{=}0-\) axis,
namely \({}^\text{slow \NFZ}I_{0-}\), the lowest number of initial \infectives
for the (non-empty) shards whose union makes up \({}^\text{slow}\NFZ\).

Focus on the slow epidemic (the arguments also work for the fast epidemic,
_mutatis mutandis_).

Consider the accept-reject procedure for deriving the initial number \({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}\)
of \infectives for the slow epidemic at algorithmic time \(2\Duration\). 
If the proposed \({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}\) lies outwith the
half-open interval
\([{}^\text{slow}\LFEInit, {}^\text{slow \NFZ}I_{0-})\)
then the proposal has to be rejected for one of the following reasons: 

(a) an epidemic begun at
\({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}<{}^\text{slow \LFE}I_{0-}\)
fails to \activate at least one conditioned \removal,
since epidemics activating all conditioned removals
\(\trianglelefteq\)-dominate \LFE, by @def-LFE;
(b) while an epidemic begun at
\({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}\geq {}^\text{slow \NFZ}I_{0-}\)
will \activate an un-conditioned \removal, since by construction
at process-time \(0\) it will infect at least one timeline
intersecting \NFZ, hence (@def-NFZ) at least one timeline
intersecting some \(\Shard{z}\) (for available in\activated \removals \(z{\in}\InnovRemAvailR\)). 
By @def-shard this would
\activate the in\activated \removal \(z\).

On the other hand suppose \({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}\) lies within
\([{}^\text{slow \LFE}I_{0-}, {}^\text{slow \NFZ}I_{0-})\).
Consider the epidemic based on an inventory
made up of \({}^\text{slow}\InnovRemCB\)
and the subset of \(\InnovInfAvail\sqcup{}^\text{slow}\OldPerpetuates\) used for the \({}^\text{slow \LFE}I_{0-}\);
this stays at initial level 
\({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}\)
till it hits \({}^\text{slow \LFE}\)
then follows \({}^\text{slow \LFE}\).
It dominates \({}^\text{slow \LFE}\), so
infects all of \({}^\text{slow}\InnovRemCB\);
by construction it will not hit
\({}^\text{slow \NFZ}\).
Consider the (potentially faster) epidemic starting from
\({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}\), augmenting the above inventory 
with _all_ \infections from \(\InnovInfAvail\) whose infectee marks do not lie in \({}^\text{slow \NFZ}\)
(so therefore the epidemic cannot
activate any \removals in \(\InnovRemAvailR\)).
This will infect all conditioned \removals of \({}^\text{slow}\InnovRemCB\) (as it dominates the previous epidemic and therefore 
\({}^\text{slow}\LFE\)).
Therefore in this case \({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}\) will be accepted.

Monotonicity of the number of initial infectives is now immediate under \CFTPmonotonicity.

:::{#thm-initial-monotonicity}
Suppose  the proposal mechanism for \({}^\text{slow}I^*_{0-,1}\), 
\({}^\text{fast}I^*_{0-,1}\) is \CFTPmonotonic,
and the previous initial numbers of \infectives satisfy
\[
{}^\text{old slow}I_{0-} \quad\leq\quad {}^\text{old fast}I_{0-}\,.
\]
Then the current _accepted_ initial numbers of \infectives satisfy
\[
{}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1} \quad\leq\quad {}^\text{fast}I_{0-,1}\,.
\]
:::

:::{.proof}


This follows from the preceding argument and \CFTPmonotonicity
(@def-initial-monotonicity),
using
\begin{align*}
{}^\text{slow}\lambda\quad=\quad{}^\text{slow \LFE}I_{0-}\,,
&\qquad
{}^\text{slow}\mu\quad=\quad{}^\text{slow \NFZ}I_{0-}\,,
\\
{}^\text{fast}\lambda\quad=\quad{}^\text{fast \LFE}I_{0-}\,,
&\qquad
{}^\text{fast}\mu\quad=\quad{}^\text{fast \NFZ}I_{0-}\,.
\end{align*}

:::

:::{.callout-warning #wrn-proposal-properties}
### Properties for proposals
It is vital  for random walk Metropolis sampling that
the random walk is skip-free; otherwise it is not hard 
to construct counterexamples
to monotonicity resulting from accept-reject.

Refer back to discussion after @def-state-and-free-innovation:
the relevant results need to be developed thereabouts.
:::


### Monotonicity for epidemics
The key theorem for \CFTP for epidemics can now be proved
by showing that \(\trianglelefteq\)-domination
of a slow epidemic by a fast epidemic is preserved
under a single step of evolution in \algorithmictime
if the same \ExtendedInnovation is used for both epidemics.

::: {#thm-nocrossover}
## Monotonicity for epidemics
Suppose that at a given algorithmic time
the \history of the slow epidemic
is \(\trianglelefteq\)-dominated by
the \history of the fast epidemic.
Then the same is true at the next epoch
(\(2\Duration\) later) of \algorithmictime.
:::

:::{.proof}
Using the accept-reject procedure analyzed in @thm-initial-monotonicity, 
the slow and fast epidemics have initial \infectives
\({}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1} \leq {}^\text{fast}I_{0-,1}\).
Let the \histories of the slow and fast epidemics be \({}^\text{slow}\History\)
and \({}^\text{fast}\History\),
so \({}^\text{slow}\HistoryInit={}^\text{slow}I_{0-,1}\)
and
\({}^\text{fast}\HistoryInit={}^\text{fast}I_{0-,1}\).
We analyze the relationship between the two epidemics
by using an argument iterating through the \chronology
\[
\Chronology\quad=\quad\InnovInfAvail\cup{}^\text{slow}\HistoryList \cup {}^\text{fast}\HistoryList
\,.
\]
Note that this chronology contains conditioned removals
\({}^\text{slow}\InnovRemCB\cup{}^\text{fast}\InnovRemCB\):
thus for some \removal times there will be two _different_ conditioned \removals, 
one from \({}^\text{slow}\InnovRemCB\) for the slow epidemic
and one from \({}^\text{fast}\InnovRemCB\) for the fast epidemic.
For such a distinct pair, the conditioned \removal from the slow epidemic will \(\preceq\)-precede
the conditioned removal from the fast epidemic, as the re-marking of the fast \removal
will give a higher target mark than for the slow \removal
(this follows because of monotonic dependence of \LFE and \NFZ on the previous epidemic).

:::{.callout-warning #wrn-conditional-removal-pair}
### Pair of conditioned removals, fast and slow
Spell out why fast \(\preceq\)-precedes slow as a consequence of monotonic dependence of \LFE and \NFZ on the previous epidemic.
:::

Tracing the evolution of these coupled epidemics through process-time
along the chronology \(\Chronology\),
and bearing in mind that the difference of the numbers of \infectives changes by no more than \(\pm1\)
at each step,
it suffices
to show the inequality \({}^\text{slow}I \leq {}^\text{fast}I\)
is maintained at
an incident \(z\in\Chronology\) if, just \(\preceq\)-before \(z\) in \(\Chronology\),
\[
{}^\text{slow}I \quad=\quad {}^\text{fast}I\,.
\]
This follows from a case-by-case analysis of \(z\).

(a) Suppose \(z\) is a \removal present in both of the \histories
(hence \activated in both, hence one of the conditioned \removals occurring in both). 
Then both \({}^\text{slow}I\) and \({}^\text{fast}I\) are decremented by \(1\)
at \(z\) and thus \({}^\text{slow}I = {}^\text{fast}I\)
remains true at \(z\).

(b) Suppose \(z\) is a \removal present in the slow \history
but not the fast \history.
Then \({}^\text{slow}I\) is decremented by \(1\)
at \(z\) while \({}^\text{fast}I\) is unchanged.
Thus \({}^\text{slow}I < {}^\text{fast}I\)
at \(z\).  
Note that the case "\(z\) is a \removal present in the fast \history
but not the slow \history" cannot arise, as this would imply the 
immediately \(\preceq\)-preceding incident \(z'\) would be the paired \removal at the same time, 
belonging to the slow \history
but not the fast \history, and therefore inductively  \({}^\text{slow}I < {}^\text{fast}I\)
at \(z'\) and so the same would be true just \(\preceq\)-before \(z\)!

(c) Suppose \(z\) is an \infection present in both \histories
(and therefore \activated in both). Now both \({}^\text{slow}I\) and \({}^\text{fast}I\) are incremented by \(1\)
at \(z\) and thus \({}^\text{slow}I = {}^\text{fast}I\)
remains true at \(z\).

(d) An \infection \(z\) need not be present in both histories: there are two ways in which
this may happen, and the first of these is that \(z\) is perpetuated in one epidemic and not in the other.

    (i) If \(z\) is perpetuated in the fast epidemic and not present in the slow,
   then \({}^\text{fast}I\) will be incremented by \(1\)
   at \(z\) while \({}^\text{slow}I\) stays constant: thus \({}^\text{slow}I < {}^\text{fast}I\) at \(z\).
    (ii) On the other hand, were \(z\) to be perpetuated in the slow epidemic
   then it would actually have to perpetuated for the fast epidemic history too. This is because we know
   \({}^\text{slow}\LFE \trianglelefteq {}^\text{fast}\LFE \trianglelefteq {}^\text{fast}\History\).
   Indeed \({}^\text{slow}I = {}^\text{fast}I\) at \(z\), so \({}^\text{slow}\LFE = {}^\text{fast}\History\)
   at \(z\), and therefore \({}^\text{slow}\LFE = {}^\text{fast}\LFE\) at \(z\). Since \(z\) is perpetuated and \activated in the
   slow epidemic, it follows that the number of infectives for \({}^\text{slow}\LFE\) is incremented by \(1\) at \(z\);
   if \(z\) is not perpetuated for the fast epidemic then the number of infectives for \({}^\text{fast}\LFE\) stays constant at \(z\);
   this would lead to failure of \({}^\text{slow}\LFE \trianglelefteq {}^\text{fast}\LFE\) at \(z\),
   contradicting @thm-LFE-monotonicity.  
   We are forced to the conclusion that if \(z\) is perpetuated in the slow epidemic then it is perpetuated in the fast epidemic also,
   and therefore \({}^\text{slow}I = {}^\text{fast}I\) at \(z\).

(e) The second way in which an \infection \(z\) need not be present in both histories is that it is forbidden by \NFZ
in one epidemic but not in the other.

    (i) If \(z\) is forbidden by the \({}^\text{fast}\NFZ\) then it must also be forbidden by the \({}^\text{slow}\NFZ\).
    This follows immediately from @thm-NFZ-monotonicity, since \({}^\text{slow}\NFZ\) is \(\trianglelefteq\)-dominated by \({}^\text{fast}\NFZ\).
    Thus here \({}^\text{slow}I = {}^\text{fast}I\) at \(z\).
    (ii) If \(z\) is forbidden by the \({}^\text{slow}\NFZ\) but not by the \({}^\text{fast}\NFZ\),
    then at \(z\) we find \({}^\text{fast}I\) is incremented by \(1\) while \({}^\text{slow}I\) remains constant,
    thus \({}^\text{slow}I<{}^\text{fast}I\) at \(z\).

It follows that crossover to \({}^\text{slow}I>{}^\text{fast}I\) cannot occur, which completes the proof of the theorem.

:::

The standard \CFTP argument can now be used to return a perfect draw from the
conditioned \SIR epidemic equilibrium: work with a sequence of 
extended innovations running backwards in time,
carry out starts at \algorithmictimes \(-2^n\Duration\) from the extreme states of fastest possible and slowest possible
epidemics (these are specified at the end of @sec-graphical
and illustrated in @fig-fastest-slowest),
and cease once the resulting fast and slow epidemics at \algorithmictime \(0\)
agree. 
@thm-nocrossover shows that
\(\trianglelefteq\)-domination
will be maintained
between successors of the 
slowest possible and fastest possible epidemics.
Moreover any other epidemic developed through 
algorithmic time from algorithmic time \(-2^n\Duration\)
using the same sequence of  \ExtendedInnovations
will remain sandwiched between the successors
of the slowest possible and fastest possible epidemics.

Note that the small set of lag \(3\), described in @thm-convergence,
guarantees eventual termination of this algorithm.
Indeed, 
let the probability of this small set occurring over times \(1-2^n\Duration,2-2^n\Duration,3-2^n\Duration\) be 
\(p>0\) (perhaps small, but positive).
If we start the \CFTP with \(n=2\) and increment \(n\) by \(1\) for each \CFTP
cycle, then almost surely the small set will eventually occur, and then
for that cycle 
the fast and slow epidemics at \algorithmictime \(0\) will agree.
(Of course in practice coalescence can be observed to occur at a much faster rate.)
